comments.author: @JayBrown-o2t
comments.text:
The main claimed value is travel time savings plus some wider economic effects, but the evidence is mixed and the numbers are heavily disputed.
The Authority’s own benefit-cost analysis projects about one hundred fourteen billion dollars in societal benefits over thirty years once Phase One runs. That breaks down roughly into seventy-six billion in user benefits—mostly faster trips between the Bay Area and LA—fifty-two billion in “wider” productivity gains from better labor markets, and smaller chunks for safety and emissions. They also point to construction jobs already created: about one hundred twenty-two thousand job-years and twenty-five billion in economic output so far, mostly in the Central Valley.
Independent researchers at UC Berkeley and UCLA come to a much lower figure. Their discounted benefits for Phase One land around twenty-seven billion against costs that push the benefit-cost ratio below one. They also find the gains skew heavily toward high-income urban areas and do little for rural or lower-income riders.
On the practical side, the first segment—Merced to Bakersfield—is projected to carry only one and a half to two million riders a year and will not cover its own operating costs. Full Phase One ridership forecasts of twenty-three to thirty million are roughly double what the Northeast Corridor carries, even though those markets are smaller. Critics, including the federal government, have called those projections unrealistic.
So the honest read: it could shave an hour or two off a San Francisco–LA trip and give the Central Valley a modest connectivity boost, but the climate impact is tiny—less than two-tenths of one percent of state emissions—and the economic case only holds if you accept the Authority’s optimistic assumptions about ridership and long-term productivity.

comments.text:
About fifteen billion dollars has been spent so far on California’s high-speed rail project.
That’s the figure from the Authority’s own 2026 business plan as of early this year. The current budget for just the first operating segment—Merced to Bakersfield—is roughly thirty-six billion, so another twenty-one billion or so is still needed for that piece alone.
Full Phase One from San Francisco to Los Angeles is now estimated anywhere from one hundred twenty-six billion up to two hundred thirty-one billion, depending on the scenario.
